wine.name: G-Max Riesling
wine.sites: Old Riesling vines, by most accounts on the limestone of the Wonnegau; the house keeps the parcel or parcels secret and names no vineyard on the label.
wine.making: Picked by hand from old, low yielding vines. By trade accounts the house ferments its dry Rieslings slowly with their own yeasts and has turned more and more to large old oak casks, Fuder, rather than steel, so the wood gives texture rather than flavour.
wine.glass: Lime oil, white peach and grapefruit pith over smoke and a salty, chalky note; dry and very tight, with high acidity, modest alcohol for its depth and a long, narrow finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and reserved on release, it needs five to ten years to open and a strong vintage keeps for two decades and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead, or let it open slowly in the glass; a white wine glass with room for air.

records.table: G-Max is Weingut Keller's dry Riesling from old vines whose parcels the house keeps secret, a wine named for two members of the family, not for a vineyard. It is taut, salty and smoky, so give a young bottle air and serve it cool, not cold.
records.story: By the house's own count the Kellers have grown vines at Dalsheim for ten generations, since 1789, and the usual account has an ancestor arriving from Switzerland that year, by the story fleeing the unrest of the French Revolution, and settling on the yellow limestone of the Hubacker. For more than a century the family sold its wine in cask; it was a forebear named Georg, as the family tells it, who first bottled the estate's Riesling, in 1921. For most of the twentieth century Rheinhessen meant sweet bulk wine, and the Kellers were growers among many. The change came in the 1990s, as a new generation took the cellar around the turn of the century, and with the 2001 vintage the estate made the first G-Max, a dry Riesling from old vines whose parcels it would not name, by one account because grapes had been stolen from the Hubacker. The name joins the present head's great grandfather, who first bottled the wine with a son of the family named Max. The estate joined the VDP in 2000, and its holdings came to include parcels in Westhofen's Morstein, Kirchspiel and Brunnenhäuschen and on the Roter Hang at Nierstein. For a sommelier G-Max is the proof that a dry German Riesling can stand at the head of a list with no vineyard on its label at all.

wine.name: Westhofener Morstein Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Morstein, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Westhofen
wine.sites: The Morstein at Westhofen, a slope facing due south up to a high plateau, on heavy clay marl with limestone in the upper layer over water bearing limestone rock that feeds the vines in drought.
wine.making: Farmed biodynamically and picked by hand. By the house's own wine sheets most of its wines ferment in traditional old oak casks, and by trade accounts with their own yeasts; the Grosses Gewächs is bottled dry after a slow fermentation.
wine.glass: Yellow plum, ripe lemon and white peach over chalk dust and a salty, stony note; dry and broad for a Riesling, with fine acidity, a touch of texture from the cask and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it closes for a few years and then gains honey, smoke and dried herbs, keeping fifteen years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour, or let it open in the glass; a white wine glass.

records.table: Wittmann's Westhofener Morstein Riesling GG comes from the Morstein, recorded at Westhofen since 1282, clay marl over limestone in the Wonnegau, farmed biodynamically. It is broad, chalky and dry, a rounder reading of the same hill that Keller also bottles.
records.story: By the family's own history its records as winegrowers at Westhofen go back to 1663, and the estate sits among the villages of the Wonnegau in the south of Rheinhessen. The vineyard behind its flagship is older on paper: the VDP records that the Morstein first appears in 1282, as Marsten, when it was given to the Cistercian monastery of Otterberg, the name probably taken from a boundary stone. Through the twentieth century the family farmed as Rheinhessen did, but it turned early to organic growing, certified, by the house's account, from 1990, and from 2004 it worked the vineyards biodynamically. As Rheinhessen's dry wines rose in the 1990s and 2000s, the VDP ranked the Morstein a Grosse Lage, with Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen and Aulerde beside it. Several houses bottle the Morstein, Keller among them, and the two side by side make a lesson in how two cellars read one hill. For a sommelier it is the clearest glass of Westhofen limestone: dry, broad and built to keep.

wine.name: Nackenheimer Rothenberg Riesling GG
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Rothenberg, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Nackenheim
wine.sites: The upper, steepest parcels of the Rothenberg at Nackenheim, slopes of up to 75 per cent above the Rhine on coarse red clayey slate of the Rotliegend, rich in iron, with little topsoil over bedrock.
wine.making: Picked by hand on the steep red slope. As the house describes its cellar, the grapes are given long contact with their skins, the wines ferment slowly with their own yeasts in oak and stainless steel and rest long on their full lees, with no additives.
wine.glass: Ripe peach, apricot and orange peel over a warm, iron and red stone note from the slate; dry, firm and darker toned than most Rheinhessen Riesling, with a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm in youth, it opens after four or five years and a strong vintage keeps for fifteen to twenty years.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white wine glass with room for air.

records.table: Gunderloch's Nackenheimer Rothenberg Riesling GG comes from the steepest red slate of the Roter Hang, the cliff the house was founded on in 1890. It is dry, firm and darker toned, peach and iron rather than lime, so decant it and pour it cool.
records.story: The red slope between Nackenheim and Nierstein is a stretch of steep red rock above the river, and the VDP records the Rothenberg at Nackenheim from 1364. In 1890 a banker of Mainz from the Gunderloch family bought vineyards there with a manor house in the village, and the house's own history dates the estate from that purchase of the Rothenberg. Nackenheim's own playwright, Carl Zuckmayer (1896 to 1977), knew the family, and by the usual account he drew on the estate for his comedy Der fröhliche Weinberg, first staged in Berlin in December 1925, with a wine grower of the Gunderloch name at its centre; the house's Kabinett carries the name Jean Baptiste after the play's grower. Through the twentieth century the estate stayed in the founder's family. In the 1980s and 1990s its sweet Rothenberg wines, up to Trockenbeerenauslese, carried its name abroad, and as the VDP built its ranking of sites the steep upper Rothenberg was classed a Grosse Lage and its dry Grosses Gewächs took the lead. A new generation took the cellar in the 2010s. For a sommelier the Rothenberg is the Roter Hang in one glass: red slate, iron and peach, dry and made to keep.

wine.making: Farmed organically with biodynamic methods and picked by hand. As the house describes its cellar, the wines ferment with wild yeasts in large wooden casks, Stück and Doppelstück, with small casks and steel beside them, with no additives or fining and a minimal addition of sulphur.

records.table: Kühling-Gillot's Niersteiner Pettenthal Riesling GG grows on the steep red slate of the Roter Hang above the Rhine, fermented with wild yeasts in large casks. It is smoky and stony, tobacco and flint over peach, and wants an hour of air.
records.story: Kühling-Gillot is a Bodenheim family estate with vines in five villages of the Rheinterrasse, from Laubenheim to Oppenheim, and by its own account the family has grown wine there for a little over two centuries. As the wine guide wein.plus tells it, the estate passed down the female line for most of that time, until a son in law, a Gillot, married into the family in 1970 and the double name joined Kühling and Gillot. The next turn came in the 2000s, when the daughter of the house married the grower of Battenfeld-Spanier in the Wonnegau; the two estates kept their names and their own vineyards but came to share a team and a way of working, organic with biodynamic methods, wild yeast fermentation and long ageing before release. On the Roter Hang the house works the Pettenthal, the Hipping, the Ölberg and the Rothenberg, where one plot of vines planted in 1934 on their own roots, by the house's account, escaped the land consolidation of the 1960s thanks to its isolated position. The Pettenthal is the house's steepest red slate between Nierstein and Nackenheim. For a sommelier its Grosses Gewächs shows the Roter Hang's smoky, stony side, a contrast to the limestone of the Wonnegau.

The house ferments with wild yeasts in large wooden casks, Stück of 1,200 and Doppelstück of 2,400 litres, with small casks and steel beside them, with no fining and minimal sulphur, and holds some wines back for years before release.

records.table: Battenfeld-Spanier's Nieder-Flörsheimer Frauenberg Riesling GG grows on a windswept ridge of pure limestone in the far south of the Wonnegau, farmed biodynamically. It is lean, chalky and cool, the stony side of Rheinhessen, and opens with an hour of air.
records.story: Battenfeld-Spanier is a young house by German measure. By its own fact sheets it was founded in 1991 at Hohen-Sülzen, in the far south of the Wonnegau near the border with the Pfalz, by a young grower of a family that had always had vines, and it was organic from the start. The wine encyclopedia wein.plus tells of a small inheritance of vineyards and, a few years on, a joining with a neighbouring estate of the Battenfeld name, which gave the house its double name. In 2005 it took its organic farming on into biodynamic methods. Its vineyards lie on limestone: the Kirchenstück around the church at Hohen-Sülzen, the Frauenberg on a windswept ridge at Nieder-Flörsheim, and the Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott at Mölsheim, close to the border with the Pfalz, all three ranked by the VDP as Grosse Lagen. In the 2000s its grower married into Kühling-Gillot of Bodenheim, and the two estates came to share a team and a cellar philosophy of wild yeast, large casks and patience, while keeping their own names and sites. For a sommelier the Frauenberg is the coolest glass of the Wonnegau: pure limestone, wind and salt.

others.name: Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott Riesling GG
others.note: From Mölsheim on the Rheinhessen side of the border with the Pfalz, limestone again, facing south south east.

traps: The Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott lies at Mölsheim in Rheinhessen; the Schwarzer Herrgott of the Zellertal over the border is a different Grosse Lage, in the Pfalz.
The Frauenberg of Battenfeld-Spanier is limestone in the Wonnegau; its Roter Hang counterparts at Kühling-Gillot are red slate, so the two houses' Grosses Gewächs show the region's two soils.
Battenfeld-Spanier and Kühling-Gillot share a team but are two estates, one on limestone in the south, one on red slate in the north.

cards.front: Battenfeld-Spanier's Frauenberg: what is the soil and the aspect?
cards.back: Limestone gravel over limestone rock, a windswept ridge facing south east to south.

cards.front: Battenfeld-Spanier: organic from its founding, in what year did it take up biodynamic methods?
cards.back: In 2005, at both its own vineyards and those of Kühling-Gillot.

questions.q: A guest compares Battenfeld-Spanier's Frauenberg with a Riesling from the Roter Hang. What sets the Frauenberg apart?
opts: A windswept ridge of pure limestone
Steep red slate above the Rhine
Sand and loess on flat land
Volcanic basalt on a south slope
questions.exp: The Frauenberg is limestone gravel over limestone rock on a windy ridge; steep red slate above the Rhine is the Roter Hang itself.

questions.q: In what year, by its own fact sheets, was Battenfeld-Spanier founded at Hohen-Sülzen?
questions.exp: The house dates itself to 1991, organic from the start; 1789 is Keller's date and 1970 the year the Gillot name came to Kühling-Gillot.

sources.title: Kühling-Gillot and BattenfeldSpanier: Philosophy and facts, BattenfeldSpanier

report: Which wine leads is not settled: the house's own site gives the Frauenberg, the Kirchenstück and the Zellerweg equal pages, and the record keeps the plan's Frauenberg; no source read sets the Zellerweg first, and since it is a Pfalz wine it would sit oddly as a Rheinhessen flagship.
The founding year 1991 is the house's own fact sheets of 2024 and 2025 with Wikipedia; wein.plus says 1998, so a refuter may test it.
The joining with a Battenfeld estate is wein.plus alone, with a year (about 1995) a second source gives as 1997, so the story tells it as wein.plus tells it with no year.
Whether the Kirchenstück and the Zellerweg are VDP.Grosse Lagen was taken from the house's naming of its GG wines, not from the VDP's own site pages; a refuter may test it.
The glass notes follow the house's own description of stone, herbs and tobacco with my own fruit notes; nobody living is named.
A Frauenberg Spätburgunder GG was dropped from others: the one listing found belongs to Keller, not to this house.

changed: story, others[1] and traps[0]: the Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott lay across the border in the Pfalz and its wine was Pfalz; now at Mölsheim on the Rheinhessen side, since the VDP's site page places it at Mölsheim in Rheinhessen near the Pfalz border, and the trap now parts it from the Schwarzer Herrgott of the Zellertal, a separate Pfalz Grosse Lage.

wine.sites and cards[0]: a hillside facing south at about 190 to 200 metres; now facing south east to south, about 190 to 270 metres, with loess and marl beside the limestone, as the VDP's site page gives it (the house says south and 190 to 200 metres).
open: The founding year 1991 stands on the house's fact sheets and its thirtieth anniversary piece of 2021; wein.plus and one trade profile say 1998.
The joining with a Battenfeld estate rests on wein.plus alone and is told as its account, with no year.
